subject: api-integration
question: Does the API receive the search term 'salt & pepper'?
ai_claim: Yes. The term is placed in the q parameter, so the API receives q = 'salt & pepper'.

ai_solution.text: The URL is built with q set to the search term.
The term is 'salt & pepper'.
The query string carries the whole term as q's value.
So the API searches for 'salt & pepper'.

failure.misconception: Inserting raw text into a query string
failure.explanation: & separates parameters in a query string, and spaces must be encoded. The server parses q=salt (with a trailing space) followed by a separate parameter named ' pepper', so it searches for 'salt '. Values must be URL-encoded: pass params={'q': term, 'page': 1} and let the client encode them (q=salt+%26+pepper).
failure.why_convincing: Terms without special characters work, which covers most manual tests.

canonical_solution: No: the & splits the value, so q becomes 'salt '. Use httpx.get(url, params={'q': term, 'page': 1}).

valid_evidence.summary: parse_qs of the query gives q = ['salt '] and a separate ' pepper' parameter.

counterexamples: The API searches for 'salt ' instead of 'salt & pepper'.

hints.text: Look for characters with special meaning in a URL.
Step 3 assumes the whole term stays in q.
& separates query parameters; values must be percent-encoded.
Parse the resulting URL's query string.
Step 3 is wrong: & ends the q parameter. Pass the term through params so it is encoded.

repair: Pass query parameters via `params={...}` so they are URL-encoded.
debrief: Building URLs with string formatting breaks on &, #, ?, spaces and non-ASCII text. Let the HTTP client encode parameters; it is correct for every input, not just the common ones.

subject: api-integration
question: If the partner's server accepts the connection but never responds, does get_rates fail quickly so checkout can fall back?
ai_claim: Yes. requests applies a default timeout, so a hung server raises an exception after a short wait.

ai_solution.text: get_rates sends a GET request.
The partner server hangs without responding.
requests times out after its default limit.
The exception lets checkout fall back quickly.

failure.misconception: Assuming the HTTP library has a default timeout
failure.explanation: requests has no default timeout: without timeout=..., it waits indefinitely for a response. A hung partner freezes the checkout worker, and enough of them exhaust the worker pool. Always pass timeout=(connect, read), e.g. timeout=(3, 5). (httpx, by contrast, defaults to 5 seconds.)
failure.why_convincing: Other clients do have defaults, and most servers respond, so the missing timeout never shows in testing.

canonical_solution: No: requests waits forever without a timeout argument. Pass timeout=(3, 5) and handle requests.Timeout.

valid_evidence.summary: Point get_rates at a server that accepts but never replies: the call blocks indefinitely.
requests documentation: 'Nearly all production code should use this parameter... requests do not time out unless a timeout value is set explicitly.'

counterexamples: A hung partner stalls every checkout request.

hints.text: Check the library's default timeout.
Step 3 assumes a default limit exists.
requests waits indefinitely unless timeout is passed.
Call get_rates against a server that never responds.
Step 3 is wrong: requests has no default timeout. Pass timeout explicitly.

debrief: Every network call needs a timeout, because 'slow' and 'never' are indistinguishable without one. Check each library's default instead of assuming; they differ.

subject: api-integration
subtopic: Sending JSON without a JSON content type
question: Will the API parse this body as JSON?
ai_claim: Yes. json.dumps produces a JSON string, and that string is sent as the request body, so the API reads JSON.

ai_solution.text: json.dumps turns the dict into a JSON string.
The string is sent as the request body.
The body is valid JSON.
So the API parses it as JSON.

failure.misconception: Assuming valid JSON text is enough
failure.explanation: Servers decide how to parse a body from its Content-Type header. Sending raw content sets no application/json header, so an API that parses by content type rejects it (415 Unsupported Media Type or a validation error) or treats it as text. Use json=body, which serialises the data and sets Content-Type: application/json.
failure.why_convincing: The bytes on the wire are exactly the right JSON, so the problem is invisible in the body.

canonical_solution: No: no Content-Type: application/json header is sent. Use httpx.post(url, json=body).

valid_evidence.summary: httpx.Request('POST', url, content=json.dumps(body)).headers has no content-type.
With json=body, the request carries Content-Type: application/json.

counterexamples: The API responds 415 Unsupported Media Type.

hints.text: Check the request's headers, not just its body.
Step 3 assumes valid JSON text is sufficient.
Servers choose a parser from the Content-Type header.
Inspect the headers of the prepared request.
Step 3 is wrong: without Content-Type: application/json the API will not parse it as JSON. Use json=body.

debrief: HTTP bodies are bytes plus a label. Getting the label wrong is as bad as getting the bytes wrong. Prefer client helpers (json=) that set both.

subject: api-integration
question: Is the export file ready to download as soon as this response arrives?
ai_claim: Yes. 202 is a success status in the 2xx range, so the export has been created and can be downloaded now.

ai_solution.text: The server responded with a 2xx status.
2xx means the request succeeded.
The request was to create the export, so the export now exists.
It can be downloaded immediately.

failure.explanation: 202 Accepted means the request was accepted for processing, which has not finished (the body even says status: queued). The client must poll the job at the Location URL (or wait for a webhook) until it reports completion and a download link.
failure.why_convincing: Most 2xx responses do mean the work is done.

canonical_solution: No: 202 means queued, not finished. Poll /reports/export/jobs/5521 until the status is complete.

valid_evidence.summary: The body reports status 'queued' for job 5521.
POST -> 202 + job 5521 -> GET job: queued -> running -> done + download URL

counterexamples: An immediate download attempt returns 404 or 'not ready'.

hints.text: Read the status code and the body together.
Step 3 assumes the work is complete.
202 Accepted means processing will happen later.
Check the status field in the body.
Step 3 is wrong: 202 means queued, not done. Poll the job URL.

repair: Poll the Location URL (with backoff) until the job reports completion.
debrief: Status codes carry precise meanings within a class. 200, 201, 202 and 204 all mean success, but only 202 says the work is still pending.

subject: api-integration
question: Is the AI right that the shared Client is faster than separate httpx.get calls for 500 products?

artifact.code:
client = httpx.Client(base_url="https://api.catalog.example", timeout=5)

def sync_products(ids):
    return [client.get(f"/products/{i}").json() for i in ids]

# Versus calling httpx.get(...) separately for each id.

ai_claim: Yes. A Client keeps connections open and reuses them, so after the first request there is no new TCP and TLS handshake per call.

ai_solution.text: httpx.get creates and closes a new connection for each call.
Each new HTTPS connection costs a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake.
A Client pools connections to the same host and reuses them.
So 500 calls pay the handshake cost roughly once instead of 500 times.

canonical_solution: Correct. Connection pooling amortises TCP and TLS set-up across requests, which is often a large share of latency for small API calls.

valid_evidence.summary: At 80 ms of handshakes per connection, 500 separate connections spend about 40 s on set-up alone.

hints.text: Count the connections each approach opens.
Step 3 describes the Client's pooling.
HTTP clients with a session or pool keep connections alive for reuse.
Estimate the handshake time for 500 new connections.
This solution is correct. Pooling avoids a handshake per request. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: For many calls to one host, use a client object (httpx.Client, requests.Session) rather than one-off functions. The speed-up comes from connection reuse, and the client is also the right place to set timeouts and headers once.
